quiz: Think about which tests are cheapest, fastest and most precise. The pyramid puts those at its wide base.
Ask whether the test checks the returned outcome or checks which calls were made. Canned answers plus outcome checks point to one kind.
Consider whether the test checks behaviour or the exact method calls. Which style survives a refactor of the internals?
Ask whether an in-memory engine behaves exactly like production in SQL dialect, data types and locking.
Container startup is the slow part. Think about how often you really need to start one and how to keep tests isolated.
Contract testing is named after the side that drives it. Which side's tests produce the pact file?
Think about what the Pact Broker stores: pacts and verification results per version. What decision can it make from those before a deploy?
Is the controller part of the domain core, or something that plugs into a port from the outside to drive the app?
Think about which layer should know about which. Frameworks and databases are details; business rules are the centre.
Ask what a bounded context is a boundary of. It is about meaning and language, not deployment or storage units.
Compare the patterns by who adapts to whom. You want to protect your model from a foreign one you cannot change.
Ask which part of the system makes the business different from its competitors and so is worth building with care.
Look for the test that runs in the pipeline without a full shared environment and checks field-level expectations between services.
interview: Describe the layers (unit, integration, E2E), why the shape is economic (speed, flakiness, cost) and give cases where a different shape fits.
Define each double by what it does: canned answers, built-in expectations, recording real calls, or a working light implementation.
Explain turning hidden inputs into injected dependencies, such as a clock and an id or random source, with fixed versions in tests.
Mention dialect, data type, locking and isolation differences, and that tests should run against the same engine and version as production.
Explain the consumer writing expectations, the contract going through a broker, provider verification, and why this beats slow shared E2E.
Cover the core with inbound and outbound ports, adapters at the edge, and the benefit: testable logic that does not depend on frameworks.
Compare the two framings, note the shared rule that dependencies point inward, and explain why they work together.
Define it as a boundary for one model and language, and mention clues like words with different meanings and team ownership.
Explain it as a translation boundary with a facade and translators, used with legacy systems, vendor APIs or messy upstream models.
List patterns such as partnership, shared kernel, customer/supplier, conformist, ACL and open host service, with when each fits.
Cover per-service unit and integration tests, contract tests at boundaries instead of a shared E2E gate, and a few smoke tests.
Explain that coverage is not verified behaviour, look at escaped bugs, and suggest fakes, real integration tests and better assertions.
Talk about executable checks like architecture tests in the pipeline, plus written decisions and context that reviewers and AI tools can follow.
